opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting contrast, and I think it's one of the more underappreciated structural differences between the two ecosystems.

In the US, there's been a pretty sharp separation over the last few years between where frontier work happens and where academia sits. The big labs, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, have pulled so far ahead on compute that most university groups simply can't train models at the scale that matters for frontier questions. A lot of the strongest PhD students get pulled into industry before they even finish, or they do internships that turn into full-time jobs. So academia here has drifted toward evaluation, interpretability, smaller-scale science, and critiquing what the labs release, and less toward building the core systems. Openness has also declined: the labs publish less, so academics often work from the outside, reverse-engineering behavior from APIs.

In China, the relationship feels much tighter, at least from what you can see in papers and author lists. Labs like DeepSeek, Qwen at Alibaba, Moonshot, and Zhipu, which itself came out of Tsinghua, hire heavily from top universities and keep close ties to them. Many students are doing real work on large models while still in school, and the line between a university lab and a company research team is blurrier. Because so many Chinese labs release open weights and fairly detailed technical reports, the academic community there gets to build directly on near-frontier models rather than watching from behind an API wall.

There's a cultural piece too. Chinese labs have leaned into publishing and openness partly as a strategy to attract talent and gain global mindshare, and that makes the pipeline from student to researcher feel more continuous.

For me, working on open models in the US, the worry is that if American academia stays compute-starved and cut off from the frontier, we lose the training ground for the next generation of researchers. That's a big part of why I care so much about fully open models here, with data, code, and training recipes released, so that universities can actually take part in the science again instead of just studying the outputs of systems they can't touch.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is something I think about a lot, because the structures are really different and they produce different kinds of research.

In the U.S., the frontier labs and academia have basically decoupled. The compute gap is so large that a university lab, even a well-funded one at Stanford or Berkeley, just can't train the models that matter at the frontier anymore. So the talent flow is mostly one direction: professors take leaves or go part-time at a lab, grad students get recruited out before they finish, and the work that comes back to academia is mostly on evaluation, interpretability, smaller-scale methods, or things like RL and post-training where you can still do meaningful work on a modest budget. There are bright spots, like the open efforts at AI2 where I work, or things like the DCLM data work, but those are exceptions and they depend on philanthropic or nonprofit funding rather than the normal academic pipeline. And a lot of what the big U.S. labs do is closed. You get a blog post and a model card, not the kind of paper a grad student can build on.

China looks quite different to me. The lines between a university, a state-backed institute, and a company are much blurrier. You have places like Tsinghua, Peking, Zhejiang feeding directly into companies like Zhipu or Moonshot or DeepSeek, and DeepSeek in particular is staffed heavily by very young researchers, many straight out of PhD programs or even undergrad, with a culture that looks more like a strong academic group than a product company. Alibaba's Qwen team publishes extensively. The incentive to publish and to release weights is much stronger, partly because that's how you build credibility when you don't yet have the brand of OpenAI or Google, and partly because the government explicitly values the ecosystem effect. So you end up with this situation where, if you're a student or researcher anywhere in the world who wants to actually read about how a frontier-ish model was trained, the most useful technical reports right now are often coming from China.

The flip side is that Chinese academia has its own constraints. Access to the best chips is restricted, so they've gotten very good at efficiency, which is a real research contribution, but it's efficiency born of necessity. And there's less of the independent, critical, safety-oriented work that U.S. academics are still pretty good at, because the institutional pressures run in a different direction.

So the way I'd summarize it: the U.S. has stronger independent academic voices but a wider moat between academia and the frontier, and China has a tighter integration between universities and labs that's produced a very open, fast-moving research culture. I think the U.S. should be a little uncomfortable about that. Openness used to be our comparative advantage, and we've been giving it up.

astra-6.text:
I think one useful distinction is how closely universities are connected to the labs doing frontier research. In the United States, there’s a lot of movement between academia and industry, but building the largest models is concentrated in companies. A professor might advise a company or take leave to join a lab, while their university group works with much more limited resources. That creates a separation between academic research and the work of training frontier models.

My impression is that in China, those boundaries can be more fluid, with professors and students participating in projects that connect universities and companies. That potentially gives academics a more direct role in model development. But I’d be cautious about generalizing: both countries have a wide range of institutions, and I know the US ecosystem better.

The underlying question is whether academics have access to the compute, engineering support, and systems they need to contribute. Having talented researchers involved matters, but their role depends a lot on what they can actually build and study.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest difference is how porous the boundary is between universities and industry. In the United States, a lot of leading researchers have moved out of universities to work full-time at AI labs. There are still collaborations and people with joint appointments, but frontier model development is increasingly concentrated inside companies, partly because of the compute and engineering resources it requires.

In China, my impression is that university affiliations are often more closely intertwined with industrial labs. Professors and their students can play a substantial role in company research while maintaining strong academic connections. So the distinction between an academic research group and an industry research team can be less clear-cut.

I wouldn’t make that an absolute distinction—there’s a lot of variation in both countries. But it does affect how talent moves, how students get involved in large projects, and how research gets shared. You have to look beyond the company name on a paper to understand the actual network of people doing the work.
